plain: Claude is an artificial intelligence assistant you talk to by typing, the way you'd send a message. Two things it's better at than anyone: swallowing very long texts (a 200-page contract, your entire novel, three years of invoices) and building things that actually work — a website, a calculator, a shop — from you describing it in your own words. It's like having a carpenter sitting next to you who's also read the entire library: you describe the piece of furniture, they build it right there in front of you, and if you don't like the door you get them to change it by just saying so. It lives on a webpage, claude.ai, and there's nothing to install.

account.free: Yes, there's a free plan and it's more than enough to learn with. It gives you a certain number of messages every five hours (no fixed number is published: it counts the size of what you send, so a big PDF costs you more than twenty short questions), with files, Projects, and Artifacts included. When it runs out, it tells you the exact time you'll have more. The Pro plan costs 20 dollars a month, which comes to around 20-22 EUR in Spain with VAT; paying for the whole year upfront brings it down to about 17 dollars a month. Pro multiplies your message allowance, unlocks the powerful model, and gives you Projects with much more capacity. Above that is Max, starting at 100 dollars a month, and it's only worth it if you're in there all day. Official prices are in dollars, so what your bank actually charges depends on the day's exchange rate.
steps: Sign in and create the account

Go to claude.ai. You'll see two buttons: 'Continue with Google' and 'Continue with email'. With Google you're in within two clicks. With email you get sent a 6-digit code you have to type into the next screen; check your spam folder, it often lands there.
Fill in your name and date of birth
It asks for your name (whatever you like: it's what Claude will call you) and your date of birth. You need to be 18 or older. This is also where you accept the terms of use.
Learn the three zones of the screen

On the left, the sidebar: 'New chat' at the top, 'Chats' below it (everything you've talked about), and 'Projects'. In the center, the big box where you type. Right below that box, on the right, the model's name: that's where you pick a brain. And at the very bottom left, your name: that's where the settings are.

Click your name at the bottom left > 'Settings' > 'Profile'. There's a box asking what preferences it should keep in mind about you. Paste this: 'Write to me in plain English, casually, with short sentences. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: explain things by what I see on screen, not by technical names. When you give me code, give it to me complete and ready to paste.' This applies to all your conversations from that point on.
Decide what it does with your conversations

In 'Settings' > 'Privacy' there's a toggle about using your chats to improve the models. Turned on, what you write can end up training the machine and is kept much longer (Anthropic talks about years). Turned off, much less is kept. Decide this now, before pasting anything from a client: turning it off tomorrow doesn't rewind today's data.
Have it build you something to see an Artifact

Go back to the text box and ask: 'Build me a one-page website for a bakery, with a header photo, three products, and a phone number'. Within a few seconds the screen splits in two and a panel opens on the right with the site running. That's an Artifact. Click the button to change it by talking: 'make the title bigger and brown'.

In the sidebar, 'Projects' > 'New project' button. Give it your idea's name. Inside there are two things that change everything: 'Project knowledge', where you upload files Claude will always have on hand, and the project instructions, where you write how you want it to work with you. Everything you discuss inside that Project starts off already knowing that.
account.warning: Two warnings before you start. One: don't paste passwords, payment keys, client tax IDs, or payroll data in there. Even with training turned off, your conversations are stored on a server that isn't yours, and deleting a chat doesn't guarantee it disappears from backups. Two: the Artifacts 'Publish' button creates a link that works for anyone who has it, no password. If you put your personal phone number in there, a price list you didn't want to show, or a client's email, that link shows it. Only publish once you've looked at the whole page with a stranger's eyes. And if you subscribe to Pro, the fee renews itself every month until you cancel it in 'Settings' > 'Billing': cancelling doesn't refund the month already charged.

first: Grab the longest document you have on hand (a contract, a manual, this year's bank statement) and drop it into the text box. Then ask it something that's only on page 80, and ask it to copy the exact paragraph. That's how you confirm with your own eyes that it read the whole thing.

Ask it to build you the dumbest possible version of your idea: 'build me a single-screen page for [your business], with a headline, three blocks, and a contact button'. When the panel opens on the right, you're already vibecoding.

Change three things by talking, one at a time: 'make the headline bigger', 'the blocks in dark blue', 'stack them one under the other on mobile'. Notice that each change creates a new version of the Artifact and that you can go back.

Click 'Copy' in the Artifact panel, open Notepad, paste, and save the file as my-site.html on the desktop. Double-click it. It opens in your browser. You've just made your first website without writing a single line.

Create a Project named after your idea, paste in the template instructions from this guide, and upload the file you just saved. From tomorrow on, start every conversation from that Project, not from scratch.
shortcuts: Enter and Shift + Enter

Enter sends the message. Shift + Enter makes a line break without sending it. You'll use this every day, because good requests run ten lines long, and people who don't know this shortcut send ten short messages and confuse the machine.
+ button to the left of the box, drag and drop, or Ctrl + V

The three ways to feed it files: the + button opens your folder (PDF, Word, Excel, photos, screenshots); dragging a file onto the box is faster and takes several at once; and Ctrl + V pastes a screenshot directly. Take the screenshot with Windows + Shift + S to crop just the part that matters. Showing it a broken screen is ten times faster than describing it.
Pencil icon over your own message

Appears when you hover over something you wrote. It lets you correct that request and relaunch it from that point, instead of typing 'no, not like that' five times. It cuts the conversation there and opens a new branch; use the < > arrows to go back to the previous one.
'Retry' button under the response

Answers the same thing again, differently. The dropdown next to it lets you ask for a 'more concise' response or switch models without retyping anything. Use it when the answer is on the right track but rambling.
'Preview' and 'Code' tabs in the Artifact panel
'Preview' shows you the site running, with clickable buttons. 'Code' shows you the letters behind it. You live in Preview 95% of the time; you only go into Code to copy.
Artifact version selector, bottom left of the panel
Shows something like 'v3' or small arrows. Every change you request creates a new version, and this takes you back to the previous one. It's your undo button when a change leaves the screen blank.
'Copy' and 'Download' buttons on the Artifact, top right of the panel
'Copy' takes the whole code to your clipboard. 'Download' saves it as a file. This is how you get your website out of Claude and onto your computer or hosting.
Model selector, below the text box

Switches between the fast brain and the powerful one. For writing text, sorting things out, and asking questions, the middle one is more than enough. For building something from scratch or unsticking a weird bug, switch to the powerful one before asking, not after.
Sidebar search
Searches by keyword across all your past conversations. Three weeks in you'll have 60 chats, and this search is the difference between finding that version that worked and starting from zero.
Your name (bottom left) > keyboard shortcut list

Claude.ai has its own list of key combinations, and it changes between versions. I won't hand you combinations from memory that might no longer exist: open it once, note the two that are useful to you, and jot them down.
daily: Drop whole long documents on it and ask specific things. Don't chop up the PDF or paste 'the important bits': it fits the whole thing, and understands better with the surrounding context. What you do need to sharpen is the question, and always ask it to copy the literal paragraph and give the page number.

Ask it to build, not to explain how to build. The right phrase is 'build me a page that...', not 'how can I build a page that...?'. The first opens a working Artifact on screen; the second gives you a tutorial you won't follow.

Change things by talking about what you see. 'The big green button below the headline, bigger, and it should say Book Now'. Never go hunting for where that is in the code. If you don't know what a part is called, describe it by where it is: 'the strip at the top', 'the box where you type your email'.

One request at a time. Ask for six changes at once and it'll get five right and one wrong, and you won't know which one broke what. One at a time, checking the preview after each. It's actually faster despite feeling like the opposite.

Always work inside a Project with its own instructions and files. It's the difference between explaining your idea from scratch every morning and sitting down to pick up where you left off. When a conversation gets stuck or slow, open a new one inside the same Project: you don't lose the context.

Show it the screen. A screenshot of the error, a screenshot of what looks wrong, a photo of a competitor's phone screen with a design you like. Paste the image and say 'I want it to look like this' or 'this is what shows up'. Saves you half an hour of describing things.

Paste the entire error message, weird characters and all. Never just 'it gives me an error'. Copy and paste the full text or take a screenshot. It fixes 90% of failures on the first try if it sees the message exactly as it appears.

templates.name: Project instructions for building without knowing how to code
templates.what: A block of text that tells Claude how to work with you inside a Project: that you don't know how to code, that everything goes in one file, that code should be given to you complete, and that it should talk about what you see on screen. This is what separates someone who builds something in an afternoon from someone who spends a week pasting pieces that don't fit. Works for any idea: website, shop, calculator, assistant.
templates.how: Sidebar > 'Projects' > 'New project'. Name it after your idea. Inside the project, find the instructions section (a button like 'Set instructions' or the project's settings icon, top right). Paste the whole text, fill in the brackets with your own details, and save. From then on, every conversation you open INSIDE that Project starts with these rules in place. Note: conversations you open outside the Project don't carry them.
fill: [DESCRIBE YOUR IDEA IN ONE SENTENCE]
What you're building and for which business, in a sentence you could say at the bar
[WHO WILL USE IT]
Your real customers: rough age, whether they come from mobile, how much patience they have
templates.code:
HOW WE WORK ON THIS PROJECT

Who I am: I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn. I describe what I want in plain English, and you write the code. I copy, paste, and check whether it works.

What I'm building: [DESCRIBE YOUR IDEA IN ONE SENTENCE: "a one-page website for my yoga studio in Austin with a schedule and a contact form"].

Who it's for: [WHO WILL USE IT: "women aged 30 to 60, mostly on mobile"].

RULES YOU ALWAYS FOLLOW:

1. Everything in ONE SINGLE file when possible. No splitting the project into folders, config files, or tools that need installing. If something needs installing, tell me first and explain why there's no other way.

2. When you give me code, give it to me COMPLETE and ready to paste. Never write "...rest stays the same" or "here goes your previous code". If the file is long, give it to me long.

3. Before writing anything, tell me in three sentences what you're going to do and wait for my go-ahead. If the change is small and obvious, just do it.

4. Talk to me about what I see on screen, not function names. Instead of "I refactored the handler", tell me "I made the send button warn when the email field is empty".

5. One change at a time. If I ask for three things, do them in three steps and pause between them.

6. When something might break, tell me before you do it: "this changes the colors of the whole page, not just the button".

7. Never put passwords, keys, or client data inside the code. If something needs a key, leave a marked placeholder and explain where it actually goes.

8. Write to me in plain English, casually, short sentences. Every technical word, translated in parentheses the first time.

9. Any text that appears on screen goes in correct English.

10. If I ask for something that's a bad idea, tell me before doing it and suggest the alternative. Don't agree with me just to agree.

WHAT I NEVER DO: touch the code by hand on my own. If a comma needs changing, give me the whole thing again.

templates.name: Project brief (context.md) to upload to Project knowledge
templates.what: A file with all the fixed information about your idea: what it is, who it's for, what colors, what phone number, what's done and what's missing. You upload it once and Claude has it in front of it in every conversation in that Project. It solves the most expensive problem in vibecoding: repeating your idea from scratch every time you open a new chat, and having each version come out different because you described it differently.
templates.how: Open Notepad (Windows) or TextEdit (Mac). Paste the text, fill in the brackets, and save the file as context.md in a folder you can find. Go into your Project, find 'Project knowledge' on the right, click the add button, and upload the file. When something important changes, edit the file on your computer, delete the old one from the project, and upload the new one: it doesn't update itself. Do this every Friday and you'll have a project that never loses track.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
What you call this when telling someone about it
What it needs to be able to do
The three things without which it's useless, in order
What it needs to look like
A real website you like, and how it should resemble it
Fixed text
Your phone, your email, your address: the real ones, exactly as you want them to appear
Current status
What already works and what you're going to ask for next

templates.name: Single-file website seed (index.html)
templates.what: A complete, working website: header with menu, big headline, three service blocks, contact form, and footer. Looks good on mobile. It's nobody's final website: it's the starting point so you stop staring at a blank screen. You paste this to Claude and from there ask for changes by talking, which is infinitely easier than starting from zero.
templates.how: Paste the entire code into a Claude conversation and write on top: 'This is my starting page. Open it in an Artifact and from now on we'll change it together. Fill in the brackets with this data: [your data]'. The panel on the right will open with the live site. You can also use it without Claude: paste it into Notepad, save it as index.html (in 'Type', choose 'All files', not 'Text document', or you'll get index.html.txt and it won't work) and double-click it.
fill: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
The name as-is, capitalized and accented however you want it read
[THE BIG LINE: WHAT YOU DO FOR YOUR CUSTOMER]
Not what you sell: what you solve for them. 'We pick up your car at home' beats 'Multi-brand garage'
[SERVICE 1/2/3]
Your three main services or products, with a price if you have one settled
--accent:#0f6b5c
Your brand color as a color code; if you don't know it, ask Claude to suggest three from your logo
[PHONE] and [EMAIL]
The real business contact details, never your personal ones unless you want everyone seeing them
templates.code:
[YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
Services Contact

[THE BIG LINE: WHAT YOU DO FOR YOUR CUSTOMER]

[A SECOND SENTENCE EXPLAINING WHO IT'S FOR AND WHERE YOU ARE]

[BUTTON TEXT: "Book now"]

[SERVICE 1]

[TWO LINES EXPLAINING WHAT'S INCLUDED AND HOW MUCH IT COSTS]

[SERVICE 2]

[TWO LINES EXPLAINING WHAT'S INCLUDED AND HOW MUCH IT COSTS]

[SERVICE 3]

[TWO LINES EXPLAINING WHAT'S INCLUDED AND HOW MUCH IT COSTS]

[CONTACT SECTION TITLE]

Write to us and we'll reply the same day.

[YOUR BUSINESS NAME] · [PHONE] · [EMAIL]
[ADDRESS OR "Online only"]

errors: "You've reached your usage limit" / "You are out of free messages until 3:00 PM"

You're out of messages until the time it tells you. It's not a bug or a punishment: the quota refills on its own every five hours. What eats up quota the most is long conversations, because every new message drags along everything before it. Trick: when a conversation passes 40 or 50 messages, ask it 'summarize where we are and what's left', paste that summary into a new chat in the same Project, and continue there. You'll spend half as much.
"Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat. Try attaching fewer or smaller files or starting a new conversation."

The conversation is full. Claude remembers everything said inside one chat, and that has a cap. There's no way to empty it: the fix is to start another one. Before you leave, ask it right there: 'Give me the complete updated code and a summary of the decisions we've made'. Copy both, open a new chat inside the Project, paste them in, and continue as if nothing happened.
"Claude hit the maximum length for a message and has paused its response. You can write Continue to keep the chat going."

The answer was so long it got cut off midway. Nothing broke. Type 'continue' and it picks up exactly where it left off. If it's code, be careful when pasting: you have to join the first chunk with the second without repeating or skipping lines. Cleaner option: type 'continue, and when you're done give me the whole file again as one piece'.

One of your messages weighs more than it can hold. Usually happens when pasting an entire book or five PDFs at once. Fix: upload the documents as attachments with the + button, instead of pasting the text into the box, and do it in two or three consecutive messages instead of one giant one.
"Claude is currently experiencing high demand" / "Overloaded" / "Internal server error"

Anthropic's servers are overloaded or something's down on their end. It's not your computer or your connection. Wait a minute and click 'Retry'. If it keeps happening, switch models in the selector: the different brains don't always get overloaded at the same time. Your conversation isn't lost.
The Artifact panel stays blank, or shows "Something went wrong"

Almost always the same thing: the page it wrote tries to pull something from outside the internet (a library, a font, a photo from another site) and the preview panel blocks it for security. Paste this: 'The preview is blank. Rewrite the whole page without depending on anything external: no outside libraries, no Google fonts, no images from other sites. Use colors and shapes made purely with code.' Usually fixed on the first try.
The code it gives you has ellipses: "// ... rest of the code stays the same as before"

It saved itself the part that didn't change, to avoid repeating itself. If you paste that into your file, the site stops working, because ellipses aren't code. Don't fix it by hand: reply 'give me the complete file, from the first line to the last, without shortening any part'. And put it in your Project instructions so it doesn't happen again.
"There was an error generating a response" when uploading a file, or the file loads forever

The file is too heavy, password-protected, or a scanned PDF that's actually just photos. Try: remove the password, split it in two, or save it as a lighter PDF. If it's a low-quality scan, screenshot the pages you care about and upload them as an image: reading images works surprisingly well.

prompts.name: Kick off your idea from zero and see it running in an Artifact
prompts.prompt: I want you to build with me [DESCRIBE YOUR IDEA: a one-page website for my hair salon, a shop to sell my ceramics, a quote calculator for my moving company]. Before you know anything else, two things about me: I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn. I'm going to describe what I want in plain English and you're going to write the code; I only copy, paste, and check whether it works. Always talk to me about what I see on screen, never about function or file names. Business context: [WHAT YOU DO AND WHERE]. Who's going to use it: [YOUR CUSTOMERS: rough age, whether they come from mobile or computer, how much of a hurry they're in]. What can't be missing, in order: first [THE MOST IMPORTANT THING], then [THE SECOND THING], and lastly [THE THIRD THING]. What I DON'T want yet: [THINGS YOU'RE LEAVING FOR LATER, e.g. user accounts or payments]. Style: it should look like [A WEBSITE YOU LIKE] but [HOW IT DIFFERS], with a [SERIOUS / CHEERFUL / PREMIUM / FRIENDLY] feel. Now do this: first tell me in five sentences what you're going to build and what you assumed, and ask me up to three questions if something is impossible to guess. Once I answer, build the whole thing in an Artifact, in a single file, with nothing that needs installing and no dependence on outside libraries or images. Make it look good on mobile. All text in correct English. When you're done, give me a list of what I can click and what's still fake.

prompts.name: Change one thing without breaking everything else
prompts.prompt: I want to change one specific thing about what you just built and I'm worried it'll break everything else. I'll describe it by what I see, because I don't know what it's called internally: [DESCRIBE THE PART BY LOCATION AND LOOK: the big green button below the headline, the strip at the top with the menu, the third box in the row of three, the form at the bottom]. What I want to happen: [THE CHANGE, DESCRIBED THE WAY YOU'D TELL A FRIEND: make it bigger and say Book Now, stack them one under the other on mobile, scroll down to the form when clicked]. Before touching anything, answer three things in plain language: what exactly you're going to change, what other parts of the page will be affected even though I didn't ask for it, and whether there's a safer way to do it than another. Then make the change and give me the complete updated file, from the first line to the last, without shortening anything and without writing anywhere that the rest stays the same. Change only this: don't take the opportunity to improve other things on your own, even if you notice something off. If you see something worth improving, note it in a separate list at the end and I'll decide. And finish by telling me what to look at in the preview to confirm with my own eyes that it worked.

prompts.name: Unstick an error when you don't understand a word of it
prompts.prompt: Something stopped working and I don't understand any of what it says. I'm giving you everything I have. What I was trying to do: [WHAT YOU WANTED TO ACHIEVE]. The last thing I asked you before it broke: [THE LAST CHANGE THAT WORKED AND THE ONE THAT CAME AFTER]. What I do to trigger it: [THE EXACT STEPS: I open the page, click the send button, and then...]. What I expected to see: [THE NORMAL THING]. What I actually see: [A BLANK SCREEN / RED TEXT / NOTHING HAPPENS WHEN I CLICK]. The error message, copied exactly, weird characters included: [PASTE THE FULL TEXT OR ATTACH THE SCREENSHOT]. Explain it to me like this: first, in two sentences with no untranslated jargon, what actually happened. Second, whether it's my fault, yours, or something external. Third, fix it and give me the complete updated file, whole, no shortcuts. Fourth, tell me exactly what to do to confirm it's fixed. And fifth, tell me what sign would have warned me earlier, so I can catch it myself next time. If you need to see something I haven't given you, ask for it by telling me where it is on screen, because I don't know how to search inside files.

prompts.name: Squeeze a huge document without trusting the summary
prompts.prompt: I'm attaching [WHAT IT IS: the tender specifications, the store's lease agreement, three years of bank statements, the machine's manual]. It's [NUMBER] pages and I'm not going to read them. I don't want a summary: summaries of big documents give me generalities that aren't useful for deciding anything. I want answers to specific questions. Here they are: 1) [SPECIFIC QUESTION, e.g.: can I subcontract part of the service and under what conditions?]. 2) [SECOND QUESTION, e.g.: what warranty period do they require and from when does it count?]. 3) [THIRD QUESTION]. For each answer I want exactly this, in this order: the answer in two plain sentences; the paragraph copied literally from the document, in quotes; the page number and section it's in; and a note saying whether the document is clear on that point or open to two interpretations. If something I ask about doesn't appear in the document, say so in those words: it doesn't appear. Don't infer it, don't fill it in with what's usually put in these cases, and don't give me a plausible-sounding made-up answer. At the end, and only at the end, add a short list of the three things in the document that could hurt me and that I didn't ask about because I didn't know they existed. All in plain English, no legalese.

prompts.name: Turn a big idea into pieces you can build one at a time
prompts.prompt: I have a whole idea in my head and I want to build it with you, but I know that if I dump it on you all at once you'll hand me back something enormous I won't even know how to look at. The idea: [DESCRIBE YOUR FULL IDEA, HOLDING NOTHING BACK, EVERYTHING YOU IMAGINE IT DOING]. My real situation: I don't know how to code, I have [HOW MANY HOURS A WEEK] available, and I want to show it to someone real before [DATE OR DEADLINE]. Budget for paid tools: [ZERO / X DOLLARS A MONTH]. Don't build anything yet. What I want is a plan broken into pieces, with these rules: each piece has to be something I can see working on screen when it's done, not an invisible internal part; each piece has to fit inside one conversation with you; and the first piece has to be the dumbest possible version that's already good enough to show someone. Give me between five and eight pieces, in order, and for each one: what I'll see when it's ready, how long you estimate it takes, what could go wrong, and the exact sentence I need to write you to start that piece. Mark which of those pieces will need money or signing up somewhere external, and how much it costs per month. And be honest about one thing: tell me which part of my idea, as I've described it, is a bad idea or doesn't hold up, and why.

words: Prompt

The instruction you write it. It's the word you'll hear most. A bad prompt is 'build me a website'; a good one says who it's for, what it needs to do, what it should look like, and what you don't want. The difference between the two is hours of your life.
Artifact

The panel that opens on the right with whatever it built, actually running. It's not a picture or an example: the buttons are clickable. It's Claude's crown jewel for someone who doesn't code, because you see the result without installing anything or knowing where each file goes.
Project

A folder with memory. Inside it you keep fixed instructions ('work with me like this') and files ('this is my business'), and every conversation you open in there starts off already knowing it. Without a Project, every morning you start from scratch explaining your idea again.
Context

Everything Claude has in front of it right now: what's been said in the chat, the Project's files, and your instructions. It's big but not infinite, and when it fills up it lets you know. That's why an old conversation gets slow and a new one flies.
Vibecoding

Building programs by talking: you describe things in plain language, the machine writes the code, you check whether it works and ask for the next change. You neither read the code nor need to. This is what this whole course is about.
Model

The specific brain answering you. Claude has three families: Haiku (fast and cheap, for simple things), Sonnet (the everyday one, what you'll use almost always), and Opus (the powerful one, for building from scratch or unsticking something hard). Version numbers change every few months; the names don't.
Hallucination

When it makes something up with total confidence: a law that doesn't exist, a function with a different name, a round number that sounds perfect. It doesn't warn you. That's why numbers, sources, and dates always get double-checked, especially when they sound just right.
Publish

The Artifact button that turns what you've built into a link that works for anyone who has it. No password. Great for showing a partner in thirty seconds; also great for handing your phone number to the internet if you haven't checked it first.
Instructions

A fixed piece of text where you tell it how to treat you. There are two places: personal ones (in Settings, apply everywhere) and Project ones (only inside that Project). Writing them once saves you repeating 'in English, short sentences, complete code' five hundred times.
Connector

A plug so Claude can talk to another program of yours: your Drive, your email, your calendar. It's great and you don't need it yet. Mentioned only so that the day you see it in the menu, you know you're not missing anything urgent.
matters: Always talk about what you see, never about code. This is the habit that decides whether you build something or give up. 'The email text box, make it warn when the @ is missing' works; hunting for where that's written yourself doesn't. The people who give up on vibecoding are almost always the ones who tried to understand the code, got overwhelmed, and concluded this wasn't for them. It never was: that's what the machine is for.

Save every working version outside of Claude. Click 'Download' or copy the code into a file on your computer and date the filename: site-march-14.html. Conversations fill up, get cut off, get tangled, and every so often a change breaks something and the good version was twelve messages back. Whoever saves goes back in a minute; whoever doesn't rebuilds a whole afternoon.

One conversation is one task. Past forty messages it starts going slow, forgetting things you said at the start, and burning through your quota twice as fast. The move: ask it for the complete code and a summary of decisions, open a new chat in the same Project, and paste both in. Costs two minutes and gives you back the fast machine.

The thing that sounds best is the thing you need to check. Claude writes with enormous confidence, and that confidence doesn't distinguish between what it knows and what it made up. If it gives you a price, a law, a deadline, or a source, verify it yourself. And before hitting 'Publish' or uploading anything to the internet, look at the whole screen with a stranger's eyes: phone numbers, emails, prices, client names. Publishing is easy; unpublishing from the mind of whoever saw it isn't.
ignore: Which exact model is best. Every few months a new one comes out with a higher number, gorgeous comparison tables, and people arguing online. The default one covers 90% of what you'll do; the day something genuinely gets stuck, switch to the powerful one and that's it. Learning to ask for things well transfers entirely to the next model. The tables expire in a month.

The API and Claude Code. The API is a long password so other programs can talk to Claude on their own, and Claude Code is a developer version you operate by typing commands into a black screen. Both are extremely powerful and both are for later. With claude.ai and Artifacts you have months of work ahead of you, and without spending money per use.

Understanding the code that shows up under the 'Code' tab. It's normal to look at it and feel like you should get it. You shouldn't. Only go in there to click 'Copy'. If curiosity ever strikes, ask it 'explain in plain English what these twenty lines do', but the way you'd read a science article: for fun, not because you need it to keep going.
